title: Pinned host buffers, UVM eviction, and fragmentation — investigative notes
content:
Summary:
This note captures a set of experiments and hypotheses around surprising OOMs and persistent GPU memory fragmentation we observed on inference hosts running mixed workloads. The unique angle here is the interaction between long-lived pinned host allocations (host-pinned buffers used for async host->device staging), CUDA Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) page migration, and the behavior of cudaMalloc/cudaMallocAsync arenas. We saw cases where device free memory slowly degraded over hours despite no apparent long-lived device tensors; the culprit appears to be pinned host pages which triggered UVM migration and prevented effective reuse of device arenas, causing fragmentation and eventual OOMs under burst load.

Context & motivation:
- Customer/benchmarks: microservice serving chat completions with variable sequence lengths and occasional large-batch embedding jobs running on the same GPU node.
- Symptoms: incremental drop in available device memory (not reported as leaked allocations by our allocator), sudden OOM when large embed batch enters, high variance in tail latency when GC/eviction occurs.
- Environment: NVIDIA A40 / A100 nodes; CUDA 12.1 in prod images; some hosts had driver 535.x. Workloads use the runtime allocator layered on top of cudamallocasync for performance.

What we measured (observations):
1) Host-pinned buffer counts correlated with device memory drop: process-level sampling showed dozens of pinned host allocations that stayed resident across requests (staging buffers, RDMA pinned pages, pinned tensors returned to user code).
2) UVM page migration spikes when pinned-host buffers are touched just before a kernel: nvidia-smi and CUPTI traces showed page migration activity and increased PCIe DMA time. After migration, device-side free lists in the allocator were fragmented into many small free regions rather than contiguous blocks.
3) cudaMallocAsync vs cudaMalloc behavior: when we replayed traces with cudaMallocAsync enabled and a properly sized arena, fragmentation was much reduced. However, when pinned host buffers force UVM to migrate pages into device address space, the async arena’s coalescing was impaired because migrated pages caused address-space scatter.
4) Timing dependence: allocations immediately after a host->device memcpy suffered most; allocations later (after a small gap) were more successful, indicating transient race between migration completion and arena reuse.
5) Long-lived host mappings prevented eviction: when a host mapping remained open, the driver kept a backing mapping and the device could not reclaim contiguous physical pages, increasing fragmentation over time.

Reproducer (high level):
- Run a small Python loop that:
  1) Allocates a large pageable tensor on the host, touches it, pins it via cudaHostRegister (or uses torch.pin_memory=True + DataLoader),
  2) Asynchronously issues a cudaMemcpyAsync to device to a transient device buffer, launches a small kernel that uses that buffer,
  3) Frees the device buffer but keeps the host pinned buffer alive in Python (simulate long-lived staging pool),
  4) Repeat with variable batch sizes and occasional large-batch spike.
- Expectation: over many iterations the device allocator free regions become highly fragmented; eventually a large allocation fails even though reported free memory sum > requested size.

Quick test commands:
- nvidia-smi --query-mem=free,used --format=csv -l 1 (observe drift)
- nsight-sys / CUPTI to capture page migration and DMA timings (filter uvm and memcpy)
- pmap /proc/<pid>/smaps to see host pinned mappings (Linux)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) UVM page migration from pinned host buffers is causing non-coalesced device mappings; the driver's page placement creates many small segments in device VA which the allocator treats as separate extents, slowing and fragmenting arenas.
2) Applications create host-pinned staging buffers with lifetimes longer than a single request and reuse them; driver keeps backing pages pinned in a way that inhibits large contiguous device allocation.
3) cudaMallocAsync's arena is effective only if device-side physical pages are contiguous/coalescable; scattered migrated pages defeat its defragmentation heuristics.
4) A race condition between migration completion and subsequent allocations can create transient throttling that leaves small holes in the free list at critical alignments.

Data to collect (telemetry additions):
- Per-process counts of pinned host pages (via /proc/<pid>/smaps or driver API).
- CUPTI timeline with uvm page migration events correlated with allocator events (alloc/free timestamps).
- Allocator free-list fragmentation histogram (size buckets) over time per device.
- Track mapping lifetimes: when a host mapping is created/pinned and when it’s unmapped.
- Kernel queue depth and outstanding H2D DMA bytes when allocations fail.

Immediate mitigations (low-risk):
- Limit application-level pinned host allocations: add guardrails in transform layers/data loader. For example cap number of pinned staging buffers per process.
- Convert rarely-reused host allocations to pageable memory; only pin per-request temporary buffers.
- Delay freeing host pinned buffers until after a short fence so migrations finish before next allocation path.

Longer-term mitigations (allocator/runtime changes):
- Preallocate a device-side staging pool sized for peak embed requests. Use pinned host pool only for staging and reuse frequently. This ensures large allocations succeed by reserving contiguous device extents.
- Add allocator instrumentation to prefer returning contiguous larger free extents when fragmentation risk is detected (defragment-on-free heuristics).
- Hunt for driver flags that control UVM migration coalescing; test with updated drivers (post-535.x) to see if migration placement improves.
- Add a migration-aware allocation mode: on detecting a recent UVM migration (via driver/CUPTI), avoid allocating large contiguous requests until a short settling period.

Experiments run (summary):
- A: Baseline workload with pinned staging pool size 10 => fragmentation and OOM after ~18k iterations.
- B: Same workload but convert host buffers to pageable (no pin) => no fragmentation for 100k iterations, but memcpy latency increased ~20%.
- C: cudaMallocAsync with arena sized to 8GB => reduced fragmentation, delayed OOM, but still observed failure when pinned host buffers were present and migration frequency high.
- D: Driver upgrade to 535.54 (experimental) showed marginal improvement in migration coalescing; still present.

Next steps / action items:
- [Ethan] add smaps/pinned-page sampling to per-process telemetry job and upload to S3 for 24h run. (JIRA-RT-8123)
- [Priya] prototype a small helper library that caps pinned staging buffers and optionally falls back to pageable memory when fragmentation risk is high.
- [Maya] implement allocator metric hooks (free-list histograms + last-migration timestamp) and expose them in the Console trace for one Dedicated test node.
- Investigate: test with CUDA 12.2/driver 540+ on a staging fleet to measure if driver-level migration improvements close the gap.

Notes / gotchas:
- Some frameworks auto-pin CPU tensors when pin_memory=True; this is easy to overlook.
- RDMA/CUDA interop (GPUDirect) can also create pinned host pages via third-party libs; check any networking stacks or RPC layers.
- Killing process does not always immediately reclaim driver-managed UVM mappings; we saw cases where only reboot/driver reset reclaimed the fragmented VA ranges.

References & links:
- Related JIRA: JIRA-RT-8123 (mem telemetry), JIRA-RT-7742 (allocator arena improvements)
- Confluence notes: serving-runtime/mem-instrumentation#pinned-uvm
- Internal trace example: s3://redwood-inference-test/traces/pinned-uvm/2024-01-10.zip

Appendix: simple Python sketch (pseudo-reproducer)

for i in range(100000):
    host = np.empty((N,), dtype=np.float32)  # pageable or pinned depending on path
    if PINNED:
        ptr = cudaHostRegister(host)
    d = cudaMalloc(size_bytes)
    cudaMemcpyAsync(d, host, size_bytes, stream=st)
    launch_small_kernel(d)
    cudaFree(d)
    # keep 'host' referenced in a global pool when simulating long-lived staging

(Replace cudaHostRegister/cudaMalloc calls with framework equivalents: torch.pin_memory, torch.empty(..., pin_memory=True), cupy.cuda.alloc, etc.)

End of note.
